# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

Working with Apptainer comes down to two steps. An image is built from a
definition file (@sec-definition-file), or pulled from a registry
(@sec-images), and programs then run in the image (@sec-running), on a cluster
usually in a job (@sec-cluster). This document covers what research software
engineers need for these steps regularly. Anything rarer, such as MPI,
overlays, or encrypted images, is in the
[user guide of Apptainer](https://apptainer.org/docs/user/latest/).
[](index.qmd) says when to use Apptainer and states the rules that hold for
every image.

On clusters that still run Singularity or SingularityCE, the commands are
mostly the same, with `singularity` in place of `apptainer`, and the
environment variables start with `SINGULARITY_` instead of `APPTAINER_`.

Checked against Apptainer 1.5.4.


# Definition files {#sec-definition-file}

A definition file, such as `analysis.def`, is the recipe of an image: a header
that names the base image to start from, and sections that say what to copy
into it, how to install the software, and how the image behaves when it runs.
Every build runs the whole file from the start, so try things out in a sandbox
first (@sec-sandbox). Keep the definition file in the repository of the code
it packages ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)).

```default
Bootstrap: docker
From: python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>

%files
    requirements.txt /opt/requirements.txt
    src /opt/analysis

%post
    pip install --no-cache-dir -r /opt/requirements.txt

%environment
    export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
    export PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1

%runscript
    exec python /opt/analysis/run.py "$@"

%test
    python -c "import numpy; print('numpy', numpy.__version__)"
    python -c "import pandas; print('pandas', pandas.__version__)"

%labels
    org.opencontainers.image.source https://github.com/lab/analysis
    org.opencontainers.image.version 1.2.0
```

- **`Bootstrap` and `From`** name the base image: `Bootstrap: docker` takes it
  from a registry, here Docker Hub, and `Bootstrap: localimage` from a SIF
  file. Pin it by its digest ([](index.qmd#sec-pin)); the registry shows the
  digest, and so does `skopeo inspect docker://python:3.12-slim`.
- **`%files`** copies files and directories from the host into the image,
  before `%post` runs. Build in the directory that holds the definition file
  and the files it copies.
- **`%post`** runs once, during the build, as root inside the image: install
  the software here, with exact versions, such as from a `requirements.txt`
  that pins every package with `==`.
- **`%environment`** sets environment variables whenever the image runs, but
  not during the build: a variable that `%post` needs is set in `%post`.
  `PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1` keeps the packages in the user's home directory out
  even when the home directory is bound (@sec-host).
- **`%runscript`** is what `apptainer run` does.
- **`%test`** runs at the end of the build (see below).
- **`%labels`** stores metadata, which `apptainer inspect --labels` shows.

Give every definition file a `%test` section that starts the main programs of
the image, for example by importing the packages of the analysis and printing
their versions. A failing test stops the build, so an incomplete image is never
written, and `apptainer test analysis.sif` runs the test again on another
machine. It shows that the image is complete, not that its results are right
([it runs](../../principles/test-types.qmd#sec-it-runs)); that is the job of
the tests of the code.


# Images {#sec-images}

An image is a single file in the Singularity Image Format (SIF), such as
`analysis.sif`: a compressed, read-only file system that holds the operating
system files, the libraries, and the programs, with metadata such as the
definition file it was built from. Copying the file copies the whole
environment, and its checksum identifies it, so record the checksum with the
results ([](index.qmd#sec-record)).


## Build an image {#sec-build}

```bash
apptainer build analysis.sif analysis.def
```

`--force` overwrites an existing image. Users without root rights add
`--fakeroot`, which makes them root inside the build without giving them any
rights outside it. Many clusters allow building only this way, or not at all.
Build where you can, on a Linux machine, in a virtual machine on macOS or
Windows, or in continuous integration, and copy the SIF file to the cluster.
Build for the processor architecture of the cluster: an image built on an ARM
machine, such as a Mac with Apple silicon, does not run on an x86 cluster.


## Pull an image {#sec-pull}

```bash
apptainer pull python.sif docker://python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>
```

`apptainer pull` downloads an image from a registry and converts it into a SIF
file. `docker://` reaches Docker Hub and the other registries of container
images, such as `docker://quay.io/lab/analysis` or
`docker://ghcr.io/lab/analysis`. Name the image by its digest, as in a
definition file ([](index.qmd#sec-pin)). Every pulled image also lands in the
cache (@sec-cache).


## Try things out in a sandbox {#sec-sandbox}

```bash
apptainer build --sandbox analysis/ analysis.def
apptainer shell --fakeroot --writable analysis/
```

A sandbox is an image as a writable directory. Because a build caches nothing,
finding out what an image needs by rebuilding it is slow. In a sandbox,
install and try things directly, as root thanks to `--fakeroot`, then write
each step that worked into the definition file and build the image from it.

Do not turn the sandbox itself into the image you use, with
`apptainer build analysis.sif analysis/`. An image changed by hand has no
recipe ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)):
`apptainer inspect --deffile` then shows only `bootstrap: localimage`, and
nobody can rebuild, fix, or update it.


## Look inside an image {#sec-inspect}

```bash
apptainer inspect --deffile analysis.sif   # its definition file
apptainer inspect --labels analysis.sif    # its labels
apptainer exec analysis.sif pip list       # its Python packages
sha256sum analysis.sif                     # its checksum
```

An image carries the definition file it was built from, so it tells what it
holds even when its source is lost. For R, `Rscript -e 'sessionInfo()'` lists
the packages instead of `pip list`.


# Running an image {#sec-running}

A program runs in an image with `apptainer exec`, `run`, or `shell`. It sees
the files of the image instead of those of the host, apart from the
directories that Apptainer binds in (@sec-binds), and it runs as the same user
as outside, with the same rights. When the program ends, nothing is left
behind, so there is nothing to start, stop, or clean up around a run.
Apptainer calls a program running in an image a *container*; its own
documentation often uses the word for the image file as well. The image is
read-only, so a program writes its results into a bound directory of the host.


## Run a program {#sec-run}

```bash
apptainer exec analysis.sif python run.py     # a command in the image
apptainer run analysis.sif --input data.csv   # its %runscript
apptainer shell analysis.sif                  # an interactive shell
```

The options go between the command and the image, and are the same for
`exec`, `run`, and `shell`:

| Option | Does |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `--containall` | Shares neither the environment, nor the home directory, nor the current directory of the host (@sec-host) |
| `--cleanenv` | Passes no environment variables of the host |
| `--no-home` | Does not bind the home directory |
| `--env NAME=value`, `--env-file file` | Sets environment variables, also with `--cleanenv` |
| `--bind src:dest:ro` | Binds the host path `src` to `dest`; `ro` read-only, `rw` the default (@sec-binds) |
| `--pwd dir` | Starts in the directory `dir` inside the container |
| `--nv`, `--rocm` | Makes the GPUs of NVIDIA or AMD available (@sec-gpus) |


## Keep the host out {#sec-host}

By default, Apptainer shares much of the host with the container: every
environment variable, the home directory, the current directory, and `/tmp`.
That is convenient for interactive work, but a step of a workflow then depends
not only on its image but also on who runs it. Run every step of a workflow
with `--containall`, so that nothing of the host reaches it that the step does
not declare.

Two leaks are common. Python loads the packages that the user installed with
`pip install --user` into the home directory before those of the image, and a
`PYTHONPATH` or an `R_LIBS_USER` set on the host does the same. The step then
computes with versions that no lock file records, on one account and not on
another: an undeclared input
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)) that defeats the pinning
of the image. `--no-home` stops the first leak, and `--cleanenv` the second;
`--containall` implies both, and isolates processes as well.

Inside a container started with `--containall`, the home directory is empty,
the current directory is not bound, and the variables of the host are gone,
including those of Slurm, such as `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`. Pass what a step needs
explicitly: data with `--bind` (@sec-binds), and variables with
`--env NAME=value` or `--env-file`.


## Bind data {#sec-binds}

```bash
apptainer exec --containall \
    --bind /scratch/project/data:/data:ro \
    --bind /scratch/project/results:/results \
    --pwd /results --env OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 \
    analysis.sif python /opt/analysis/run.py --input /data/samples.csv
```

`--bind source:destination` makes a directory of the host visible inside the
container, and `:ro` makes it read-only. Bind only the directories a step reads
and writes, and its inputs read-only: a step that sees only its declared inputs
fails loudly when it reaches for anything else, and an input bound read-only
cannot be changed by mistake
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-mutation)).

Bind to fixed paths inside the container, such as `/data` and `/results`, not
to the paths of the host: the commands inside the container are then the same
on every machine, and only the binds change.


## Use GPUs {#sec-gpus}

`--nv` makes the NVIDIA GPUs of the machine, or those a job was granted,
available in the container, together with the driver of the host. The image
brings CUDA and the libraries built on it, and the host brings the driver, so
the CUDA version in the image must be one that this driver supports;
`nvidia-smi` on the host shows the newest it supports. `--rocm` does the same
for AMD.


# On a cluster {#sec-cluster}

On many clusters, Apptainer is a module, which `module load apptainer` loads,
in a job script as well. Build the images elsewhere (@sec-build), and keep
them, like the data, on a scratch or project file system.


## Run in a Slurm job {#sec-slurm}

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

module load apptainer

srun apptainer exec --containall \
    --bind "$SCRATCH/data:/data:ro" --bind "$SCRATCH/results:/results" \
    --env OMP_NUM_THREADS="$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" \
    "$SCRATCH/images/analysis.sif" \
    python /opt/analysis/run.py --input /data/samples.csv
```

A job runs Apptainer like any other program, and Slurm grants the resources.
The variables of Slurm do not reach a container started with `--containall`
(@sec-host), so pass what the program needs with `--env`, such as the number of
threads; the shell of the job expands `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` before Apptainer
starts.

Workflow managers, such as Nextflow and Snakemake, start each step in its image
themselves. Give them the options of @sec-host through their settings for
Apptainer, `apptainer.runOptions` in Nextflow and `--apptainer-args` in
Snakemake.


## Keep the cache off your home directory {#sec-cache}

```bash
export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$SCRATCH/apptainer/cache"
export APPTAINER_TMPDIR="$SCRATCH/apptainer/tmp"
mkdir -p "$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" "$APPTAINER_TMPDIR"
```

Apptainer keeps every image it pulls in a cache, `~/.apptainer/cache` by
default, and unpacks images for a build in `/tmp`. Both grow by gigabytes,
while the home directories and `/tmp` of clusters are small, and a full quota
makes later jobs fail with errors far from the cause. Put the lines above into
`~/.bashrc`, with the scratch or project directory of your cluster.
`apptainer cache list` shows the cache, and `apptainer cache clean` empties it.
